topics.title: Minibeasts
topics.intro: Minibeasts are small creatures like insects, spiders, snails and worms. Insects always have six legs and three body parts.
topics.teach: Explain why a spider is not an insect.
topics.talk: Go on a minibeast hunt: look under stones and logs, then put them back gently.

topics.title: Dinosaurs and prehistoric life
topics.intro: Dinosaurs ruled the Earth for millions of years, long before people. We know about them from fossils.
topics.teach: Explain how we can tell what a dinosaur ate from its teeth.
topics.talk: Visit a museum (or a book) and ask {him} which dinosaur {she} would most like to meet.

c.note: flat or peg-like teeth: Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Diplodocus

topics.title: Hot and cold places
topics.intro: Places near the Equator are hot. Places near the Poles are cold. Animals and people have clever ways to live in each.
topics.teach: Explain how a camel is suited to the desert.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would pack for a trip to the Arctic, and to the Sahara.

head: Place
What it is like
Who lives there
visual.caption: Hot near the Equator, cold near the Poles.

topics.title: Countries of the world
topics.intro: There are about 200 countries in the world. Let’s find some of the biggest and most famous on the map.
topics.teach: Name a country in each of three continents.
topics.talk: When you see where something was made (“Made in China”), find that country on the map.

topics.title: Seasides and rivers
topics.intro: The UK is made of islands, so the sea is never far away. Rivers start in the hills as streams and flow down to the sea.
topics.teach: Explain the journey of a river from the hills to the sea.
topics.talk: At the beach or a river, ask {him} to point out physical and human features.

topics.title: Exploring space
topics.intro: People have walked on the Moon, lived on space stations and sent robots to Mars. Space exploration is one of humanity’s greatest adventures.
topics.talk: Look up when the International Space Station flies over your home, and watch for it together.

events: Yuri Gagarin: first person in space
Neil Armstrong walks on the Moon
Tim Peake goes to the space station

topics.title: Light and shadows
topics.intro: We need light to see. Light travels in straight lines. When something blocks the light, it makes a shadow.
topics.teach: Explain how a shadow is made.
topics.talk: Make shadow puppets on the wall with a torch.

topics.title: Sound
topics.intro: Every sound is made by something vibrating (shaking very fast). The vibrations travel to our ears.
topics.teach: Explain how a drum makes a sound.
topics.talk: Put rice on a drum or a tin lid and watch it jump when you make a noise.

topics.title: Electricity
topics.intro: Electricity powers lights, toys and even some racing cars. It flows round a complete circuit, like cars round a track.
topics.teach: Explain why a bulb only lights when the circuit is complete.
topics.talk: Count the things in one room that use electricity. Which use batteries?

items.prompt: How many legs does an insect have?
items.explain: All insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

items.prompt: How many legs does a spider have?
items.explain: Spiders have 8 legs, so they are not insects. They are arachnids.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT an insect?

options.feedback: Ants have 6 legs: insects.
Bees have 6 legs: insects.
Ladybirds are beetles: insects.

items.explain: Spiders have 8 legs.

items.prompt: How do earthworms help gardens?

options.feedback: Worms eat dead leaves and soil, not living weeds.
Birds love eating worms!

items.explain: Worm tunnels let air and water reach plant roots, and their poo makes the soil rich.

items.prompt: What does a snail carry on its back?
items.explain: A snail’s shell is its home and protection.

items.prompt: Where are you most likely to find woodlice?
items.explain: Woodlice like dark, damp places.

items.prompt: Why are bees so important for plants?

options.text: They water the flowers each day
options.feedback: Bees carry pollen.

options.text: They eat the pests on the leaves
options.feedback: Ladybirds do that! Bees carry pollen.

items.explain: This is called pollination. Without bees, many fruits wouldn’t grow.

items.prompt: Put the life cycle of a ladybird in order.
items.explain: Like butterflies, ladybirds go egg, larva, pupa, adult.

items.prompt: A stick insect looks just like a twig. What is this called?
items.explain: Camouflage helps animals hide from predators.

items.prompt: A dinosaur had sharp, pointed teeth. What did it probably eat?

options.feedback: Plant-eaters had flat or peg-like teeth for chewing or stripping leaves.
All animals need food.

items.explain: Sharp teeth are for tearing meat. T. rex had teeth as long as bananas!

items.prompt: A dinosaur that ate only plants was a…
items.explain: Stegosaurus, Triceratops and Diplodocus were herbivores.

items.prompt: Which famous dinosaur had huge jaws, big back legs and tiny arms?
items.explain: T. rex was one of the biggest meat-eating dinosaurs.

items.prompt: Which dinosaur had three horns on its face?
items.explain: Tri means three: Triceratops means “three-horned face”.

items.prompt: Which dinosaur had big plates along its back and spikes on its tail?
items.explain: Stegosaurus used its spiky tail to defend itself.

items.prompt: Did people and dinosaurs live at the same time?

options.text: No: dinosaurs were long before people
Yes: people kept them as pets
options.feedback: Only in films! There were no people then.

options.text: Yes, in the Stone Age, in caves
options.feedback: Stone Age people lived long after the dinosaurs.

items.explain: The last dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. The first humans appeared much, much later.

items.prompt: What does “extinct” mean?

options.feedback: It means none are left.

options.text: Too big to live in a zoo
options.feedback: Extinct animals can be any size.

items.explain: Dinosaurs are extinct. So is the dodo.

items.prompt: What do most scientists think helped wipe out the dinosaurs?
distractors: a big flood all over the world
items.explain: A huge asteroid hit the Earth about 66 million years ago, changing the weather all over the world.

items.prompt: Pterosaurs flew in the sky at the time of the dinosaurs. What did they use to fly?
items.explain: Their wings were stretched skin, a bit like a bat’s.

items.prompt: A very dry place with very little rain is called a…
items.explain: The Sahara in Africa is the biggest hot desert.

items.prompt: How is a camel suited to the desert?

options.text: It can go a long time without water
It has thick blubber like a seal
options.feedback: Blubber is for cold seas. A camel’s body is built to save water.

options.text: It swims to find water to drink
options.feedback: There is very little water in a desert!

items.explain: Camels store fat in their humps and can go days without water.

items.prompt: How is a polar bear suited to the Arctic?

options.text: Thick fur and fat keep it warm
It sleeps in the warm sun all day
options.feedback: The Arctic is cold: it needs fur and fat.

options.text: It has thin skin to stay cool
options.feedback: It needs to stay warm, not cool.

items.explain: White fur also helps it hide in the snow.

items.prompt: A hot, wet forest near the Equator is called a…
items.explain: The Amazon rainforest in South America is the biggest.

items.prompt: The cold area around the North Pole is called the…
items.explain: Polar bears live in the Arctic. Penguins live in the Antarctic, at the other end!

items.prompt: Would a penguin ever meet a polar bear in the wild?

options.text: No: they live at opposite ends

options.feedback: They live at opposite ends of the Earth!
Polar bears never go anywhere near the hot Equator.

items.explain: Polar bears: Arctic (north). Penguins: Antarctic and southern seas.

items.prompt: Why is it hot near the Equator?

options.text: The Sun shines straight down there
It is much closer to the Moon
options.feedback: The Moon doesn’t heat the Earth.
It is because of the Sun.

items.explain: Direct sunlight is strongest, so the Equator is hot all year.

items.prompt: Inuit people in the Arctic used to build winter shelters from blocks of snow. What are they called?
items.explain: Snow traps air, so an igloo keeps people surprisingly warm.
This is the UK, where we live: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
France is our neighbour, across the English Channel. Its capital is Paris.
The USA is a huge country in North America. Astronauts went to the Moon from here.
China has more people than almost any other country, and the Great Wall of China.
India is in Asia. Tigers and elephants live there.
Brazil is in South America. Most of the Amazon rainforest is here.
Australia is a country AND a continent. Kangaroos live here.
Egypt is in Africa. The ancient Egyptians built the pyramids beside the River Nile.
Kenya is in Africa, on the Equator. Lions, giraffes and zebras live on its grasslands.
Japan is a country made of islands in Asia. It has super-fast bullet trains.
Canada is the second biggest country in the world, north of the USA.
Russia is the biggest country in the world. It stretches across Europe and Asia.
Italy is shaped like a boot! The ancient Romans came from here.
Spain is in Europe, south of France. It is often hot and sunny.

items.prompt: Which is the biggest country in the world?
items.explain: Russia is so big it has 11 time zones!

items.prompt: Which country is just across the English Channel from England?
items.explain: You can go through the Channel Tunnel by train to France.

items.prompt: Which country is shaped like a boot?
items.explain: Look at a map: Italy kicks a ball (the island of Sicily)!
The Thames flows through London to the North Sea.
The Severn is the longest river in the UK.
The Trent flows through the middle of England.

items.prompt: Where the land meets the sea is called the…
items.explain: The UK has a very long coast because it is made of islands.

items.prompt: Where a river starts is called its…
items.explain: Rivers often start as small streams in the hills.

visual.caption: A river starts at its source and flows downhill to its mouth.

items.prompt: Where a river meets the sea is called its…
items.explain: The mouth of the Thames is near the North Sea.

visual.caption: A river starts at its source and flows downhill to its mouth.

items.prompt: Which way does a river always flow?

options.feedback: Water flows downhill.
Rivers flow downhill to the sea or a lake.

items.explain: Water always flows downhill, so rivers run from the hills to the sea.

visual.caption: A river starts at its source and flows downhill to its mouth.

items.prompt: A high, steep rock face by the sea is called a…
items.explain: The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk.

items.prompt: What is a lighthouse for?

options.text: To warn ships about dangerous rocks
To light up the beach for swimmers
options.feedback: It shines out to sea for ships.
It is a tower with a bright light.

items.explain: The flashing light warns sailors at night.

items.prompt: Which is a HUMAN feature at the seaside?

options.feedback: Cliffs are made by nature.
Dunes are formed by the wind.

items.explain: Piers, harbours and lighthouses are built by people.

items.prompt: Who was the first person ever to go into space, in 1961?
items.explain: Yuri Gagarin, from the Soviet Union (he was born in what is now Russia), orbited the Earth once in 1961.

items.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
items.explain: In 1969, on the Apollo 11 mission.

items.prompt: Who was the first British astronaut, in 1991?
items.explain: Helen Sharman was a chemist who went to the Mir space station.

items.prompt: Which British astronaut lived on the International Space Station in 2015 and 2016?
items.explain: Tim Peake even ran a marathon on a treadmill in space!

items.prompt: What is the International Space Station?

options.text: A train station on the Moon
options.feedback: It flies around the Earth.

options.text: A rocket launch pad in Florida
options.feedback: It is in space, not on the ground.

items.explain: Astronauts from many countries live there for months at a time. You can sometimes see it from your garden!

items.prompt: Why do astronauts float inside the space station?

options.text: They are falling round the Earth
There is no air inside it
options.feedback: There IS air inside the station; that is not why they float.
They float because they and the station are falling round the Earth together.

items.explain: The station and everything in it falls around the Earth at the same speed, so everything floats.

items.prompt: How have scientists explored Mars?

options.text: By sending astronauts to live there
options.feedback: No person has been to Mars yet. Maybe you will be the first!
Mars is too far away for that: we send rovers.

items.explain: Rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance drive around Mars taking photos and studying rocks.

items.prompt: What do we need to launch astronauts into space?
items.explain: Only rockets are powerful enough to push all the way up through the air and reach space.

items.prompt: What do we need to be able to see things?
items.explain: Without light we can’t see anything: dark is the absence of light.

items.prompt: How is a shadow made?

options.feedback: That is reflection.
Shadows need light!

items.explain: Light travels in straight lines. If something blocks it, there is a dark patch behind: a shadow.

items.prompt: Which of these is a LIGHT SOURCE (it makes its own light)?

options.feedback: The Moon only reflects the Sun’s light.
A mirror reflects light; it doesn’t make it.

items.explain: Light sources: the Sun, fire, a torch, a light bulb.

items.prompt: Why should you never look straight at the Sun?
items.explain: The Sun’s light is so strong that it can hurt your eyes. Never look straight at it, even with sunglasses on.

items.prompt: When is your shadow longest on a sunny day?

options.text: At midday, when the Sun is high
options.feedback: At midday your shadow is shortest.

options.text: It is always the same length
options.feedback: Watch it change through the day!

items.explain: A low Sun makes long shadows; a high Sun makes short ones.

items.prompt: How are all sounds made?

options.feedback: Light helps us see, not hear.
Sound comes from vibrations.

items.explain: Touch your throat while you hum: you can feel the vibrations.

items.prompt: Which part of your body do you hear with?
items.explain: Vibrations travel through the air into your ears.

items.prompt: What happens to a sound as you walk away from it?

options.feedback: Sounds get fainter with distance.
The pitch stays the same; the volume drops.

items.explain: The further away you are, the quieter it sounds.

items.prompt: Could you hear a rocket explosion in empty space?

options.text: No: there is no air in space

options.feedback: Sound needs something to travel through, like air.

options.text: Only if it happens at night
options.feedback: Day or night, there is no air in space to carry sound.

items.explain: Sound needs air (or water or a solid) to travel. Space is silent!

items.prompt: A short guitar string makes a high note. What does a long string make?

options.feedback: Longer strings vibrate more slowly: lower notes.
It still vibrates and makes a sound.

items.explain: Short = high, long = low.

items.prompt: Why does a bulb only light when the circuit is complete?

options.text: The bulb needs to warm up first
options.feedback: It is about the loop being complete.

options.text: Batteries only work in the dark
options.feedback: Batteries work any time.

items.explain: Like cars on a track: if there is a gap, they can’t get round.

items.prompt: Which material lets electricity flow through it?

options.feedback: Plastic is an insulator: that is why wires are covered in it.
Dry wood is an insulator.

items.explain: Metals are conductors. Copper is used in wires.

items.prompt: What gives a torch the power to light up?
items.explain: Batteries store electricity for things we carry about.

items.prompt: Which is a safe thing to do?

options.text: Keep electric things away from water

options.feedback: Never! Mains electricity can kill.

options.text: Fly a kite near the power lines
options.feedback: Power lines are very dangerous.

items.explain: Water and electricity are a dangerous mix.

items.prompt: What does a switch do in a circuit?
items.answer: it opens or closes a gap
distractors: it changes the colour of the light
items.explain: A switch breaks or completes the circuit.
